rows.a: Electrical discharge machining is widely used for nickel‑based superalloys such as Hastelloy because these alloys are difficult to machine by conventional methods (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Shastri et al. 2022). The physical and mechanical properties of the electrode material therefore directly affect both process economics and component quality: tool electrode properties influence process efficiency (material removal), machining accuracy and surface roughness (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024). Electrode wear is a primary concern because high tool wear reduces dimensional fidelity of the electrode, increases tooling cost, and alters discharge conditions during machining; studies report tool wear rate (TWR) as a key metric and relate it to electrode material and operating parameters (Shastri et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2022). Experimental work on graphite electrodes shows a trade‑off controlled by graphite grain size: coarser graphite (10 µm) gives higher process efficiency but higher relative tool wear, while finer graphite (1 µm) yields lower surface roughness and can reduce tool wear under the tested conditions (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024). Mechanistically, detached graphite grains influence the stability of electrical discharges and thus the efficiency and consistency of material removal (Nowicki et al. 2024). Process parameters that govern these outcomes have been identified: discharge current and pulse duration are the dominant factors for material removal rate (MRR) and surface roughness (Ra), while the pulse interval (time between discharges) strongly affects relative electrode wear for graphite electrodes (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024). Complementary factorial studies report peak current as the single most influential factor for both Ra and MRR in treated and untreated superalloy samples (Nas & Kara 2022). Current and pulse duration have also been implicated in shaping electrode geometry during machining, with unstable sparks and heat diffusion transforming sharp electrode edges into rounded or hemispherical ends and increasing wear at edges and surfaces (Ramabalan et al. 2024). Surface integrity after EDM is the second major concern: researchers evaluate not only Ra and recast layer formation but also broader surface integrity effects, and have investigated mitigation strategies such as cryogenic treatment, powder‑mixed EDM, ultrasonic assistance and electrical discharge coating to improve surface characteristics and reduce adverse effects (Shastri et al. 2022)(Liew et al. 2020).
rows.b:
Electrical discharge machining is widely used for nickel-based superalloys such as Hastelloy, which are difficult to cut by conventional means; in EDM, material is removed by electrical discharges between the workpiece and the tool electrode, and the physical and mechanical properties of the electrode directly influence process efficiency, machining accuracy, and surface roughness (Nowicki et al. 2022). Graphite electrodes are increasingly implemented due to low raw material cost, good machinability, and high sublimation temperature, and studies on Hastelloy C-22 show that discharge current and pulse duration are the principal drivers of material removal rate and surface roughness, while the time interval dominates relative tool wear of graphite electrodes (Nowicki et al. 2022). Consistent with the central role of electrical parameters, analysis on a corrosion-resistant superalloy using full-factorial tests and Taguchi optimization found peak current to be the most influential factor for average surface roughness and material removal rate by ANOVA at 74.79% and 86.43%, respectively, with optimal combined settings observed for the shallow-cryogenically treated workpiece at 6 A and 300 μs pulse-on time (Nas & Kara 2022).

The choice of electrode material shapes both the cost and the quality of the process through its wear behavior and the surfaces it produces. For graphite, grain size conditions the trade-off between efficiency, wear, and roughness: larger-grain graphite yields higher process efficiency but incurs higher relative tool wear, while the smallest grain size achieves the lowest surface roughness on Hastelloy C-22 (Nowicki et al. 2022). Under negative polarity and with newly engineered fine-grained graphites, EDM with fine grains has been reported to increase process efficiency and reduce tool wear; moreover, grains detached from the electrode influence discharge stability and process efficiency, and predictive models have been proposed to select parameters for desired efficiency, tool wear rate, and surface roughness (Nowicki et al. 2024). Beyond average wear metrics, electrode geometry degradation is also critical: during square-hole machining of Hastelloy B2, current and pulse duration strongly affect wear at surfaces and edges, and unstable sparks with heat diffusion can transform sharp-ended square electrodes into hemispherical ends, altering feature fidelity and cutting time (Ramabalan et al. 2024).

Surface integrity after machining is the second concern this review examines. High tool wear rate, low material removal rate, and high surface roughness are persistent challenges, and studies investigating hybrid or assisted EDM approaches evaluate not only MRR and TWR but also surface integrity and the recast layer formed during machining (Shastri et al. 2022).

rows.a:
Selective laser melting (SLM) builds near-net-shape, complex-geometry metallic components directly from powder by selectively melting and fusing powder layers with a high-power laser; the process can produce near-full-density parts (up to 99.9% relative density) and is applicable to a range of metals due to recent laser developments (Yap et al. 2015).

Post-build heat treatments alter the SLM maraging-steel microstructure in multiple, measurable ways: SLM as-fabricated parts can develop extremely fine submicron grains and in situ precipitation (for example, needle-shaped Ni3X nanoprecipitates that produce age hardening), and deliberate heat treatments further change precipitate characteristics, relieve residual stresses, and modify mechanical anisotropy (Tan et al. 2018)(Haghdadi et al. 2020). Heat treatments that approach intercritical temperatures can also induce martensite-to-austenite reversion, producing reversed austenite largely at martensite-lath boundaries (Khan et al. 2022).

Compared with the extensive literature on mechanical performance and fatigue, corrosion behaviour of SLM maraging steels is less comprehensively understood: reviews and studies note gaps in understanding of fatigue and other performance metrics for SLM steels, which parallels a limited and still-developing body of work on corrosion (Afkhami et al. 2019)(Haghdadi et al. 2020). Where corrosion-related studies exist, they show that prior heat treatment and microstructural state strongly affect corrosion outcomes—for example, intercritical tempering that produces reversed austenite and local Ni enrichment is reported to enhance pitting resistance, (Khan et al. 2022) and thermochemical treatments such as plasma nitriding improve wear and corrosion resistance only when combined with appropriate prior heat treatments (nitriding without prior aging can produce cracks in the compound layer) (Godec et al. 2021).
rows.b:
Selective laser melting builds near net-shape metallic components by selectively melting and fusing powder layers with a high power-density laser, achieving up to 99.9% relative density and enabling economically viable, near–full-density parts with complex geometries (Yap et al. 2015). Metal additive manufacturing similarly produces complex engineering parts in a layer-by-layer manner using a high-energy source, reinforcing SLM’s suitability for intricate designs (Haghdadi et al. 2020).

Heat treatment after printing modifies the SLM microstructure and properties: in grade 300 maraging steel, the as-fabricated state exhibits an average submicron grain size of 0.31 μm, indicative of cooling rates up to 10^7 K/s, while aging induces massive needle-shaped Ni3X (X = Ti, Al, Mo) nanoprecipitates that drive age hardening via Orowan bowing and coherency strain mechanisms; heat treatments also relieve residual stresses and slightly reduce mechanical anisotropy (Tan et al. 2018). Intercritical tempering within the α′ + γ range at 720°C promotes reversed austenite, which nucleates mainly along martensite lath boundaries due to local Ni enrichment from the dissolution of intermetallic particles (Khan et al. 2022). This reversed austenite improves corrosion performance in 3.5 wt% NaCl, with the 720°C-tempered condition showing a higher pitting potential, lower corrosion current density, and lower corrosion rate than as-printed, aged, and homogenized specimens without reversed austenite (Khan et al. 2022). AM can also act as an intrinsic heat treatment that triggers in situ phase transformations in precipitation-hardened steels, further linking processing history to microstructural evolution (Haghdadi et al. 2020).

While reviews have primarily emphasized mechanical properties of SLM parts, corrosion has been addressed through targeted studies (Yap et al. 2015). For example, comprehensive evaluations on SLM maraging steel include corrosion resistance alongside impact and tribological performance across as-fabricated and heat-treated states (Tan et al. 2018). Plasma nitriding at 520°C for 6 h can enhance wear and corrosion resistance, but nitriding without prior aging leads to cracks in the compound layer, whereas prior heat treatment enables the additive-manufactured steel to benefit from the thermochemical process (Godec et al. 2021). Broader assessments of AM steels report that unique microstructures with hierarchical (sub)grains and fine precipitates can enhance corrosion resistance compared to conventional counterparts, even as achieving acceptable ductility and fatigue performance remains challenging (Haghdadi et al. 2020). Fatigue behavior, in particular, is identified as an area with significant knowledge gaps relative to other properties and processing parameters in SLM steels (Afkhami et al. 2019).

rows.a: India has set ambitious national targets for solar deployment, including a goal to expand renewable capacity to 175 GW by 2022, of which 100 GW is solar and 40 GW is expected from grid‑connected rooftop PV (Goel 2016). Financial barriers are the most frequently discussed constraint: studies report that upfront cost and perceived financial risk reduce household willingness to invest in rooftop PV, while subsidies and lower operating costs reduce that initial investment barrier (Parsad et al. 2020). Specifically, subsidy programs act as a primary motivator because they help households overcome the initial risk of investing in a new technology, and low prices combined with low maintenance costs reduce long‑run apprehension about returns and upkeep (Parsad et al. 2020). Empirical analyses using structural equation modelling and artificial neural networks identify financial incentives (subsidies) and cost‑related factors as among the strongest motivators of household PV investment (Parsad et al. 2020). Survey evidence from another regional study likewise finds that solar PV cost has a negative effect on willingness to adopt, and that perceived risk related to the investment also deters uptake (Tanveer et al. 2021). Non‑financial barriers matter as well: limited knowledge and awareness and technical barriers are shown to play a significant role in forecasting investor decisions, indicating that lack of information and perceived technical complexity reduce adoption rates (Parsad et al. 2020). Social and behavioural factors such as social norms and household self‑efficacy can increase willingness to adopt, suggesting that peer effects and confidence in managing the technology mitigate non‑financial constraints (Tanveer et al. 2021). Broader studies of household and community solar additionally highlight equity, spatial and institutional issues—including supply‑chain and business‑practice problems—that interact with trust and access, implying that concerns about fairness, installer reliability, and system governance can further slow household uptake (Sovacool et al. 2022). Complementary reviews of India’s renewable sector identify multiple systemic constraints that hinder diffusion despite strong solar resources, reinforcing that financial, informational, technical and institutional obstacles together limit rooftop adoption (Khare et al. 2013)(J & Majid 2020).
rows.b: India has set ambitious targets for rooftop solar within its broader renewable energy goals, including 175 GW by 2022 with 100 GW from solar and 40 GW specifically from grid-connected rooftop PV, and studies discuss the issues and challenges in achieving these targets and the policy instruments in place (Goel 2016). Evidence from Kerala based household surveys using two datasets (237 and 387 households) shows that, within a risk–return logic, government subsidies operate as the primary motivator by offsetting the initial investment risk, while lower prices and low maintenance costs further mitigate concerns about long-term returns; the strongest motivators combine environmental considerations with financial incentives via PV subsidies, and, in forecasting adoption decisions, an ANN model fed by SEM outputs ranked technical barriers alongside knowledge and awareness as significant predictors (Parsad et al. 2020). Comparative regional evidence from Pakistan aligns on the salience of financial and non-financial determinants: social norms, perceived self-efficacy, and beliefs about PV benefits positively affect willingness to adopt, whereas perceived risk and PV cost exert negative effects and openness to technology is insignificant (Tanveer et al. 2021). At the system level, reviews of India’s renewable sector note constraints hampering development despite favorable solar resources and the prospect of grid parity, underscoring that barriers extend beyond pure economics (Khare et al. 2013); broader assessments likewise identify obstacles alongside strong policy support and investment opportunities, indicating that challenges persist even amid enabling policies (J & Majid 2020). Complementing these finance- and awareness-centered accounts, mixed-methods research on household solar adoption outlines equity and justice concerns—demographic, spatial, interspecies, and temporal—that interact with deployment, implying that policy and business practices must attend to these risks as adoption scales (Sovacool et al. 2022).

rows.a:
Mobile health applications have been proposed as a low-cost support for diabetes self-management, a proposition supported by the rapid proliferation of health apps—estimated at no fewer than 40,000 in 2012 and exceeding 100,000 by 2014—which has created a large, accessible supply of tools that could be deployed at low marginal cost compared with face-to-face services (Boulos et al. 2014)(Zhao et al. 2016).

Randomized and non-randomized trials have sought to quantify the effect of these apps on glycaemic control. Some early and small studies of specific apps (for example, BlueStar) reported reductions in hemoglobin A1c in limited samples, but a multicenter pragmatic randomized controlled trial of BlueStar did not detect a difference between intervention and control arms at 3 months for the primary outcome of HbA1c (mean difference −0.42, 95% CI −1.05 to 0.21; P =.19) (Agarwal et al. 2018). An exploratory analysis from that trial did, however, associate greater individual app use with modest improvements in HbA1c: each additional day of app use over the study period corresponded to a $0.016$‑point decrease in 3‑month HbA1c (95% CI −0.03 to −0.003), indicating a dose–response relation between usage intensity and glycaemic outcome among users (Agarwal et al. 2018).

Mechanisms by which apps are intended to affect glycaemia include promotion of self‑monitoring, immediate feedback on glucose trends, individualized decision support, and behavioral incentives. Self‑monitoring is the most commonly applied behavior‑change technique reported in reviews of app interventions (Zhao et al. 2016). In pilot work with adolescents using an app that combined automated glucometer data transfer, trend analysis, prompting, social features and gamified rewards, daily blood‑glucose measurement frequency rose by 50% (from 2.4 to 3.6 measurements per day; P =.006, n = 12), illustrating how design features that reduce friction and add incentives can increase proximal self‑management behaviours that plausibly mediate glycaemic benefit (Cafazzo et al. 2012).

Despite these potential mechanisms, engagement commonly declines after the first weeks. Qualitative research identifies multiple barriers to continued use—such as lack of perceived usefulness, burdensome interaction, concerns about credibility and privacy, and mismatch with user needs—and conversely highlights motivators and design elements that sustain use, including ease of use, real‑time feedback, personalization, reminders, goal setting, and credible information (Peng et al. 2016). Systematic reviews similarly report heterogeneous study quality and persistent risk of bias, while noting that interventions incorporating real‑time feedback, individualized elements, and health‑professional involvement tend to show stronger behaviour‑change signals (Zhao et al. 2016). Moreover, pragmatic trials find that contextual factors (for example, clinical site) substantially affect how much participants actually use apps, and low overall usage may explain null average effects on HbA1c in some trials (Agarwal et al. 2018).

Taken together, the evidence indicates that apps can change self‑management behaviours when they achieve sustained, sufficiently frequent use through features such as automated data transfer, feedback and incentives, but real‑world effectiveness on glycaemic control is inconsistent and appears contingent on user engagement and contextual implementation (Cafazzo et al. 2012)(Agarwal et al. 2018)(Zhao et al. 2016).

Microfinance is widely promoted as a pathway to women’s empowerment and entrepreneurship, though the empirical record is mixed (Banerjee & Jackson 2016)(Huis et al. 2017). Evidence from a mixed-method study comparing 132 female entrepreneurs with 238 non-entrepreneurs found entrepreneurs scored higher on economic, social, political, and psychological indicators of empowerment, with relatively smaller gains in political and, to an even lesser extent, social domains; interview data corroborated these patterns and suggested that directing microfinance toward women’s entrepreneurship—and ensuring women’s full control over their ventures—may be critical to realizing empowerment benefits, although non-entrepreneurs also exhibited social empowerment; the authors note limits to generalizability given the restricted geography and respondents’ high illiteracy (Khan et al. 2022). In contrast, an ethnographic study of three Bangladeshi villages found that microfinance increased indebtedness among already impoverished communities and exacerbated economic, social, and environmental vulnerabilities, while undermining social capital—highlighting conditions under which credit can worsen rather than alleviate constraints (Banerjee & Jackson 2016).

Context and mechanism matter: research in North India shows that innovative business processes in a rural social enterprise that both enabled women’s economic activity and complied with local social and cultural norms contributed to empowerment and to changing the social order, framing emancipatory social entrepreneurship as processes that empower women and reshape the norms that constrain their agency (Haugh & Talwar 2014). Conceptually, a three-dimensional model distinguishes personal (micro), relational (meso), and societal (macro) empowerment and posits that time lags and cultural context shape when and how these effects emerge, implying that access to credit alone is insufficient without attention to sequencing, culture, and the specific dimension targeted by an intervention (Huis et al. 2017). At the industry level, heterogeneity in institutional missions and financing also conditions outcomes: while commercial investment supports scale, institutions with strong social missions—often using subsidies—are better positioned to reach the poorest, and market forces “cannot fill all gaps,” underscoring why credit expansion may not translate into empowerment for the most marginalized without mission-aligned design (Cull et al. 2009). More broadly, the microfinance field spans issues of sustainability, products and services, management practices, clientele targeting, regulation and policy, and impact assessment, indicating that program design features beyond credit access are central to women’s enterprise and empowerment outcomes (Brau & Woller 2004).
